Series::sigmoid¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sigmoid() const -> Series
Series& Series::sigmoid_()

What It Does¶

sigmoid() applies the logistic map elementwise:

σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e^{-x})

Every real input is squeezed into the open interval (0, 1).

That gives sigmoid() a very different feel from relu(): it never produces a hard zero-or-pass gate, and it never exceeds 1.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, containing the logistic value for each input lane.

Gradient¶

If y = σ(x), then:

  • dy/dx = σ(x) (1 - σ(x))

So the derivative is largest around x = 0 and shrinks toward the saturated ends.

In-Place Form¶

sigmoid_() is the in-place sibling of sigmoid(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.sigmoid_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5, 0.73105858]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Large negative input lands near 0, zero lands at 0.5, and large positive input lands near 1.

std::cout << pluss::series::print(pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0}).sigmoid()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.1192, 0.5000, 0.8808]

Example 2. The reverse pass multiplies by σ(x)(1 - σ(x)).

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.sigmoid();
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.11920292, 0.5, 0.88079708]
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.10499359, 0.25, 0.10499359]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • sigmoid() never hard-clips, but it does saturate toward 0 and 1.

  • Because the derivative is σ(x)(1 - σ(x)), the slope is strongest near the middle and weaker near the tails.

  • There are no axis toggles or broadcasting branches here; it is purely elementwise.

Summary¶

Use sigmoid() when each lane should be mapped smoothly into (0, 1).

See Also¶

  • Series::relu: hard rectification instead of smooth squashing.

  • Series::tanh: another smooth elementwise nonlinearity with a different output range.
